title: Observability and Monitoring (Prometheus, Grafana, Tracing)
summary: This day covers essential concepts for building AI engineering skills.
content:
# Observability and Monitoring (Prometheus, Grafana, Tracing) ##### "The automation is slow" — but which part? A support ticket said orders were taking "a few minutes" to appear in the CRM instead of seconds. The engineer on call had logs, and the logs said the workflow completed successfully every time. The path involved five hops: a webhook receiver, a Redis queue, a Python worker, an enrichment API, and the CRM write. Each component logged its own success. None of them knew about the others. Finding the slow hop meant correlating timestamps across five log streams by eye, which took most of an afternoon. The culprit turned out to be connection-pool exhaustion in the worker — invisible in every individual log line, obvious in a single trace. **Monitoring tells you something is wrong. Observability lets you ask why without deploying new code.** For distributed automation stacks, that difference is the difference between a twenty-minute investigation and an afternoon. ##### The three pillars **Metrics** are numeric time series — cheap to store, ideal for dashboards, trends and alerting. They answer *"how many, how fast, how often?"* but cannot tell you about one specific request. **Logs** are discrete events with detail. They answer *"what exactly happened to order ORD-1042?"* Expensive at volume, essential for forensics. **Traces** follow one request across every service it touches, showing the timing of each hop as nested spans. They answer *"where did those four minutes go?"* — the question the opening story could not answer. Google's Dapper paper established the model that OpenTelemetry now standardizes. Use all three, and connect them: a metric alert points you at a time window, traces in that window show the slow hop, and the trace ID takes you to exactly the right log lines. ##### Prometheus metrics Prometheus **scrapes** a `/metrics` endpoint your service exposes. Four metric types matter: - **Counter** — monotonically increasing (requests, errors). Query with `rate()`. - **Gauge** — goes up and down (queue depth, active connections). - **Histogram** — bucketed observations enabling percentile queries (latency). - **Summary** — client-side quantiles; prefer histograms, which aggregate correctly across instances. ```python from prometheus_client import Counter, Histogram, Gauge, make_asgi_app from fastapi import FastAPI app = FastAPI() WEBHOOKS = Counter( "automation_webhooks_total", "Webhooks received", ["provider", "event_type", "outcome"], # labels: low cardinality only ) PROCESSING = Histogram( "automation_processing_seconds", "End-to-end processing time", ["workflow"], buckets=(0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2.5, 5, 10, 30, 60), ) QUEUE_DEPTH = Gauge("automation_queue_depth", "Pending items", ["queue"]) EXTERNAL_CALLS = Counter( "automation_external_calls_total", "Third-party API calls", ["service", "status_class"], ) app.mount("/metrics", make_asgi_app()) @app.post("/webhooks/stripe") async def stripe_webhook(request: Request): with PROCESSING.labels(workflow="order_sync").time(): try: event = await verify_and_parse(request) await enqueue(event) WEBHOOKS.labels("stripe", event["type"], "accepted").inc() return Response(status_code=202) except SignatureError: WEBHOOKS.labels("stripe", "unknown", "rejected").inc() raise HTTPException(401) ``` **Label cardinality is the trap that kills Prometheus installations.** Every unique label combination is a separate time series. `event_type` has maybe 20 values — fine. Adding `order_id` would create one series per order, and a few hundred thousand series will exhaust memory and make queries unusable. **Never label with IDs, emails, or URLs containing IDs.** Those belong in logs and traces. Useful PromQL for automation dashboards: ```promql # Success rate over 5 minutes sum(rate(automation_webhooks_total{outcome="accepted"}[5m])) / sum(rate(automation_webhooks_total[5m])) # p95 latency by workflow histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le, workflow) (rate(automation_processing_seconds_bucket[5m]))) # Third-party error rate sum(rate(automation_external_calls_total{status_class="5xx"}[5m])) by (service) # Queue growing faster than it drains — the backlog predictor deriv(automation_queue_depth[10m]) > 0 ``` n8n exposes its own metrics at `/metrics` when you set `N8N_METRICS=true`, giving workflow execution counts, durations and failures. Scrape it alongside your services so one dashboard covers the whole stack. ##### Structured logging and aggregation Logs become useful at scale only when they are **structured** and **correlated**. ```python import structlog structlog.configure(processors=[ structlog.contextvars.merge_contextvars, structlog.processors.add_log_level, structlog.processors.TimeStamper(fmt="iso", utc=True), structlog.processors.JSONRenderer(), ]) log = structlog.get_logger() # Bind once per request; every subsequent log line carries these fields structlog.contextvars.bind_contextvars( trace_id=trace_id, request_id=request_id, tenant=tenant, workflow="order_sync", ) log.info("order_processed", order_id="ORD-1042", duration_ms=284, items=3) ``` The critical field is **`trace_id`**. With it, you can jump from a slow span in Grafana Tempo directly to the log lines for that exact request. Without it, you are back to correlating by timestamp. Ship logs to **Loki** (label-based, integrates natively with Grafana, cheap) or the **ELK stack** (full-text search, heavier). Set retention deliberately — 7 to 30 days is typical — and **never log secrets or full personal data**; redact at the logger, not by remembering. ##### Distributed tracing with OpenTelemetry Tracing is what solves the opening story. A **trace** is one request's journey; each **span** is one operation within it, with timing and attributes, nested to show causality. ```python from opentelemetry import trace from opentelemetry.sdk.trace import TracerProvider from opentelemetry.sdk.trace.export import BatchSpanProcessor from opentelemetry.exporter.otlp.proto.grpc.trace_exporter import OTLPSpanExporter from opentelemetry.instrumentation.fastapi import FastAPIInstrumentor from opentelemetry.instrumentation.httpx import HTTPXClientInstrumentor from opentelemetry.instrumentation.psycopg import PsycopgInstrumentor provider = TracerProvider() provider.add_span_processor(BatchSpanProcessor(OTLPSpanExporter(endpoint="http://tempo:4317"))) trace.set_tracer_provider(provider) # Auto-instrumentation: HTTP, database and outbound calls traced for free FastAPIInstrumentor.instrument_app(app) HTTPXClientInstrumentor().instrument() PsycopgInstrumentor().instrument() tracer = trace.get_tracer(__name__) async def process_order(event: dict) -> None: with tracer.start_as_current_span("process_order") as span: span.set_attribute("order.id", event["order_id"]) # high cardinality is FINE here span.set_attribute("tenant", event["tenant"]) with tracer.start_as_current_span("enrich_customer"): customer = await enrich(event["email"]) # nested span, timed with tracer.start_as_current_span("write_crm") as crm_span: try: await crm.upsert(customer) except Exception as exc: crm_span.record_exception(exc) crm_span.set_status(trace.StatusCode.ERROR) raise ``` Note the asymmetry with metrics: **high-cardinality attributes belong in traces**, not metric labels. Traces are sampled and stored per-request, so `order.id` is exactly the right thing to attach. Two operational details. **Context propagation** carries the trace ID across service boundaries via HTTP headers (`traceparent`) — inject it when publishing to a queue and extract it in the worker, or your trace breaks at the async boundary. And **sampling**: trace 100% in staging, 1–10% in production, but always sample errors and slow requests (tail-based sampling). ##### Dashboards and SLOs An **SLI** is a measurement, an **SLO** is the target, and the **error budget** is the allowed shortfall. ```text SLI: proportion of webhook events processed successfully within 60 seconds SLO: 99.5% over a rolling 30 days Error budget: 0.5% ≈ 3.6 hours of failure per 30 days ``` The error budget reframes reliability usefully: if you have consumed 10% of it, ship features; at 90%, stop and fix reliability. It turns "is this reliable enough?" from an argument into arithmetic. A dashboard worth having shows, per workflow: success rate against the SLO line, p50/p95/p99 latency, throughput, error breakdown by type, queue depth and consumer lag, third-party API error rates and latency, and cost per run where applicable. Structure it so the top row answers "is anything wrong?" in three seconds. ##### Alerting Alert on **symptoms users experience**, not on every internal anomaly. High CPU is not an alert; a breached SLO is. ```yaml # alerts.yml groups: - name: automation rules: - alert: WebhookSuccessRateBelowSLO expr: | (sum(rate(automation_webhooks_total{outcome="accepted"}[15m])) / sum(rate(automation_webhooks_total[15m]))) < 0.995 for: 10m # avoid alerting on brief blips labels: { severity: critical } annotations: summary: "Webhook success rate {{ $value | humanizePercentage }} (SLO 99.5%)" runbook: "https://wiki.internal/runbooks/webhook-failures" - alert: QueueBacklogGrowing expr: automation_queue_depth > 500 and deriv(automation_queue_depth[10m]) > 0 for: 15m labels: { severity: warning } annotations: summary: "Queue {{ $labels.queue }} at {{ $value }} and growing" - alert: NoWebhooksReceived expr: sum(rate(automation_webhooks_total[30m])) == 0 for: 30m labels: { severity: critical } annotations: summary: "No webhooks in 30 minutes — silent failure suspected" ``` That last rule is the **silent-failure detector**, and it catches what error alerts structurally cannot: an integration that stopped receiving events entirely. Every alert should carry a **runbook link**; an alert without one wastes ten minutes per incident on orientation. Route by severity through Alertmanager — critical pages, warning goes to Slack, info to a daily digest — and use `group_by`, `repeat_interval` and inhibition rules so one incident produces one notification rather than forty. ```mermaid flowchart LR A[FastAPI service] -->|/metrics| P[(Prometheus)] B[n8n N8N_METRICS=true] -->|/metrics| P C[Workers] -->|/metrics| P A & B & C -->|OTLP spans| T[(Tempo)] A & B & C -->|JSON logs| L[(Loki)] P & T & L --> G[Grafana
dashboards + SLOs] P --> AM[Alertmanager] AM -->|critical| PD[PagerDuty] AM -->|warning| S[Slack] G -.trace_id links.-> L ``` ##### Common pitfalls - **High-cardinality metric labels** — IDs in labels will take Prometheus down. - **Alerting on causes rather than symptoms**, producing noise nobody reads. - **No `for:` duration**, so a five-second blip pages someone. - **Logs without a trace ID**, forcing timestamp correlation. - **Broken context propagation** across queue boundaries, splitting traces in half. - **100% trace sampling in production**, at significant storage cost. - **Secrets or PII in logs and span attributes.** - **Dashboards nobody looks at** — if it is not on a wall or in a daily review, alert on it instead. - **No silent-failure alert** for absence of traffic. - **Alerts without runbooks or owners.** ##### Your hands-on tie-in The practical task: instrument a FastAPI service with **Prometheus metrics and OpenTelemetry traces**, build a **Grafana dashboard showing success rate and p95**, and add an **Alertmanager rule that pings Slack on SLO breach**. Then break something on purpose — point an outbound call at a dead host — and watch the whole chain fire: the metric moves, the trace shows a failing span, the alert reaches Slack. An alert you have never seen fire is not yet an alert. The mini project is that observability stack applied across your whole automation setup, including scraping **n8n's metrics endpoint** so workflow executions appear on the same dashboard as your service. Add trace context propagation through your Redis queue so a webhook and its worker processing appear in one trace — that single change is what makes "which hop is slow?" answerable in seconds. For the assignment, **define one SLO and an Alertmanager rule that pings Slack when the failure rate breaches it**. Write the SLO precisely — the SLI definition, the target, the window and the resulting error budget in minutes — and include a runbook link in the annotation. Then state what you would do at 10%, 50% and 90% budget consumption; that policy is what makes an SLO a decision tool rather than a number on a dashboard. ##### Key takeaways - Metrics say what is wrong, logs say what happened to one request, traces say where the time went — connect them with a shared trace ID. - Keep metric labels low-cardinality; put IDs and emails in traces and logs, never in Prometheus labels. - Use histograms for latency so percentiles aggregate correctly, and propagate trace context across queue boundaries or traces break. - Define SLIs and SLOs with an explicit error budget, and alert on user-visible symptoms with a `for:` duration and a runbook link. - Always include a silent-failure alert on absence of traffic — it catches the outages that error-rate alerts cannot see.
